questions.q: What shape does a function you write yourself follow, matching every built-in cmdlet you've used since Lesson 3?
options: Verb-Noun, e.g. function Test-DiskSpace
Noun-Verb, e.g. function DiskSpace-Test
camelCase with no hyphen, e.g. function testDiskSpace
PowerShell functions have no naming convention at all
questions.explain: Every cmdlet, and every function you write, should follow the Verb-Noun pattern for consistency.

questions.q: What does a typed parameter like [int]$ThresholdGB do?
options: It rejects a call that passes the wrong kind of value, catching the mistake immediately at call time
It converts every value passed to a string automatically
It has no real effect and exists purely as documentation
It prevents the parameter from ever having a default value
questions.explain: Typing a parameter enforces what kind of value is acceptable, failing fast instead of failing confusingly deep in the function body.

questions.q: Why did calling Test-DiskSpace with no arguments at all still work in the example?
options: Because $ComputerName and $ThresholdGB both had default values supplied in the param block
Because PowerShell functions never require any parameters
Because the function ignored its parameters entirely
Because Test-DiskSpace is a built-in cmdlet, not a custom function
questions.explain: = $env:COMPUTERNAME and = 20 are default values that apply automatically when the caller doesn't supply that argument.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why does the Verb-Noun convention matter even for a function nobody else will ever call?
options: Consistency compounds — a function that breaks the pattern is a small tax on every future reader, including yourself months later
PowerShell will refuse to run a function that isn't named Verb-Noun
It has no real benefit and is purely a cosmetic preference
Verb-Noun naming is only required for functions published to the PowerShell Gallery
questions.explain: The lesson argues readability and predictability, not a technical enforcement requirement.

questions.q: What does Chapter 3 conclude with, and what does Chapter 4 add next?
options: Chapter 3 closes with functions; Chapter 4 (PowerShell for Azure & SQL) covers the Az module, connecting to Azure, dbatools, and a real automated script
Chapter 3 closes with the Az module; Chapter 4 covers if/else and switch
Chapter 4 repeats Chapter 3's content with no new material
This is the final chapter of the course, with nothing coming after it
questions.explain: Chapter 3 built the general scripting toolkit; Chapter 4 is where it gets pointed specifically at Azure and SQL Server work.
